analysis.one_liner: Shields businesses and health care entities from lawsuits over COVID-19 infections during the emergency.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2020 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the federal COVID-19 public health emergency, this bill would have barred lawsuits for damages against businesses, nonprofits, schools, and health care entities by anyone who caught COVID-19 at their premises or through their services — including employees and contractors. The shield would apply as long as the business followed federal or state reopening guidelines and CDC mitigation steps like masks, cleaning, distancing, and temperature checks. The only exception was for conduct a court found to be gross negligence, a very high bar; lawsuits by government regulators were still allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Virtually every business — corporations, partnerships, sole proprietors, farms, nonprofits, and schools — plus health care entities treating or testing COVID-19 patients and manufacturers and distributors of protective equipment. If the bill passed, a customer, worker, or patient who caught the virus at a business could not sue for damages unless they proved gross negligence, and businesses facing reopening costs would be spared the expense and risk of infection lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses, schools, health providers, and PPE makers

how_it_helps.text: It exempts businesses and COVID-19 medical entities from any punitive, compensatory, or general damages in civil suits arising from an individual contracting COVID-19 during the public health emergency [S2][S3].
The shield covers not just customers but also employees, contractors, and anyone else who enters a business, and it applies to suits in both federal and state court [S3].
It protects the full range of business structures — corporations, partnerships, LLCs, sole proprietorships, and farming cooperatives — as well as nonprofits and educational institutions [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to relieve businesses already strained by pandemic closures from further economic strain from civil tort claims as they reopen [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers, customers, and patients who contract COVID-19 at a business or health care entity would lose their right to compensation through the courts unless they could prove gross negligence — a standard far higher than ordinary carelessness. The cost of the infections themselves, and of any unsafe workplace practices short of gross negligence, would fall on the sickened individuals and their families.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and customers sickened at businesses

drawbacks.text: The shield removes a key legal incentive for businesses to keep workers and customers safe: someone who caught a potentially deadly disease at work or a store could not recover damages unless the conduct rose to gross negligence, which courts treat as reckless disregard far beyond ordinary carelessness [S2][S3].

Because compliance is measured against state or federal reopening guidelines and CDC mitigation steps, a business that merely followed written guidance would be immune even if its own circumstances made that guidance inadequate — and the shield would cover health care entities and protective-equipment makers as well [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection: without protection, businesses feared opportunistic lawsuits over infections that are hard to trace, which could have discouraged reopening and added insurance costs during an economic crisis [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift real risk from businesses to the people most exposed to the virus. Some liability certainty for struggling businesses during a pandemic is a legitimate goal, but this version was broad: it covered every kind of business and medical entity, extended to employees as well as customers, and left the only recourse through the near-impossible gross-negligence standard. Weaker workers and sickened customers would have borne the cost, and employers would have had less reason to go beyond minimum written guidance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 8, 2020 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kelly Loeffler introduced the bill in the Senate on June 8, 2020 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and that was the last action recorded for the entire Congress [S5].
The bill received no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and never became law [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers, customers, and patients kept their ability to sue businesses and health providers under state law if they caught COVID-19 on the premises — and businesses gained nothing, since the shield never took effect. The concentrated interests the bill was written for ended up no worse off than before, but not protected either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sickened workers and customers who kept suing rights

for.name: Sen. Kelly Loeffler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 8, 2020 to shield businesses and health care entities from COVID-19 infection lawsuits.

for.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Made broad COVID-19 liability protection for businesses a central Republican demand in the 2020 pandemic relief negotiations, of which this bill was one piece.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after its June 8, 2020 referral and died in committee.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a hearing or vote during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no measurable support from either party.

industries.industry: Broad business community (retail, restaurants, hospitality, and employers generally)
industries.note: The bill would have immunized virtually all businesses from damages suits by workers, customers, or visitors who caught COVID-19 on their premises, as long as they followed reopening guidance and CDC steps like masks and cleaning. That transfers the cost of infections from businesses to the sickened individuals, whose only remaining route was the near-impossible gross-negligence standard.

industries.industry: Health care entities and medical equipment/PPE manufacturers
industries.note: Entities treating, testing, or transporting COVID-19 patients, and businesses manufacturing or distributing protective and medical equipment, would be shielded from suits by patients, employees, and others. This would limit accountability for providers and suppliers serving people at their most vulnerable during the pandemic.

Personal-injury lawyers would lose a large category of potential cases — infection claims against businesses and medical entities. Their interest in keeping those claims alive runs alongside sickened workers' and customers' ability to recover.

A blanket liability shield would remove infection claims from the books that liability insurers price and pay. The savings would accrue to insurers and their business customers rather than to the people who got sick.
